definition: Partisanship means strong, one-sided loyalty to a party or faction.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word partisanship. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know partisanship should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Pure partisanship decides the family's game nights now: the Ramirez cousins vote as a bloc, whatever the question.
Favoritism is one unfair preference at a time — smaller than partisanship, which pledges the whole judgment to a side.
Zealotry goes further than partisanship: loyalty hardened into fanaticism that admits no question at all.

Tribalism is group loyalty so strong it overrides individual judgment — my people, right or wrong. Partisanship is the same surrender aimed at a party, faction, or bloc: the side does the judging. Tribalism names the instinct; partisanship gives it a party badge.

Factionalism is infighting: rival blocs inside one organization, each loyal to itself first. Partisanship is the loyalty a single member gives one of those sides. A club suffering factionalism has split into camps; a member showing partisanship votes with a camp every time.

A bias is a tilt in judgment, and it can be unconscious — a judge may not know she has one. Partisanship is declared and worn openly: standing allegiance to a side that settles every question in advance. Bias leans; partisanship has already signed up.

In the 1890s our town had two newspapers, and partisanship was their entire business model.
The Ledger was Republican; the Beacon was Democratic.
Neither ever conceded that the other side had won an argument, a bet, or a ballgame.
Historians who compare their coverage of the same flood find two different disasters: each paper blamed the mayor only when he belonged to the other party.
Subscribers chose a paper the way they chose a church, and canceling was apostasy.
The town got its first weather page in 1911, when a new editor decided the temperature, at least, could be nonpartisan.
